title: Data Analysis Design by Example
text:
Overview
The best way to learn design in any field is to study examples. These lessons therefore build small versions of real data analysis pipelines to introduce some fundamental ideas in data science and show how experienced data scientists think.
Greg Wilson is a programmer, author, and educator based in Toronto. He was the co-founder and first Executive Director of Software Carpentry and received ACM SIGSOFT’s Influential Educator Award in 2020.

start where you are · use what you have · help who you can

title: 1  Introduction
text:
The best way to learn data analysis is to study examples, so these lessons build small versions of real analysis pipelines — each of a different kind — rather than reimplementing the tools those pipelines use. This lesson defines what a pipeline is (ingest, clean, explore, model, communicate), introduces the running example — a web service and its operations — and sets the through-line: we use mature tools and build analyses, not libraries.

A data analysis pipeline is a chain of small, checkable steps.
There are many kinds of analysis; this course samples them rather than drilling one.
We use mature tools (Polars, DuckDB, Vega-Altair, httpx) instead of rebuilding them.
Reproducibility means recording every step so an analysis can be re-run and audited.

title: 2  An Event Log Generator
text:
Build the primary dataset: a web service’s event stream — a table of users and a table of events (requests, signups, deployments, errors) linked to them by user ID, generated from seeded randomness and written as CSV. This is the first of two generators; later lessons analyze its output and can check their answers against the truth it encodes.

A seed makes pseudo-random numbers reproducible.
Synthetic events let us know the “right answer” (for example, which version was slower).
A generator documents the assumptions baked into the data.
CSV is a simple, portable exchange format.

title: 3  Your First Pipeline
text:
Build a small end-to-end exploratory pipeline: read the event log, clean the obvious problems, summarize it (requests per endpoint, latency, error rate), and plot the result. Along the way, meet the tools this course relies on — reading CSV, selecting and filtering columns, grouping and joining, reshaping, and computing basic statistics — as libraries to call, not things to reimplement.

A pipeline is ingest → clean → explore → summarize → communicate.
Polars reads CSVs and does select, filter, group, join, and reshape for us.
Basic descriptive statistics come from the library, not hand-rolled code.
Every pipeline ends by checking its answer, ideally against known truth.

title: 4  Data Dictionaries and Provenance
text:
Build the metadata layer of a pipeline: a data dictionary that records each field’s name, type, units, meaning, and allowed values — for fields such as timestamp, endpoint, status_code, and latency_ms — and a provenance log that records each step’s inputs and outputs.

Metadata (data about data) is data too.
A data dictionary is a contract between producer and consumer.
Provenance lets someone reconstruct how a result was derived.
Reproducibility is impossible without provenance.

title: 5  A Data Cleaning Pipeline
text:
Build a cleaning pipeline that profiles the raw event log, deduplicates records, normalizes status codes and endpoint names, fills missing values, and validates the result — emitting a clean dataset and a data-quality report. Cleaning is its own kind of analysis: quality assurance.

Cleaning is a pipeline of small, testable transformations.
Profiling first (types, ranges, missingness) tells you what needs fixing.
Deduplication needs a notion of “same record”.
Every change is documented so clean data can be traced to raw data.

title: 6  An Operational Metrics Generator
text:
Build a generator that produces time-series metrics for the service — request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, CPU, and memory — with trend, seasonality, noise, and a few injected anomalies, so the forecasting and monitoring lessons have known targets to find.

A time series is trend plus seasonality plus noise.
Because we choose the components, we know the true signal.
Injected anomalies give the monitoring lesson known targets to recover.

title: 7  A Cohort and Retention Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that groups users into cohorts by signup month and computes how many of each cohort return in each later month — the retention curve. A distinct kind of analysis: behavior over time, by group.

A cohort shares a defining event; retention tracks its members over time.
Grouping by cohort and period is a table joined to itself.
Retention answers “do users come back?”, not just “how many signed up?”.
Check counts against hand-computed small examples.
crumbs: 7  A Cohort and Retention Pipeline

title: 8  A Funnel Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that traces users through a sequence of stages — signup, activation, first deploy, paid plan — and reports the drop-off at each one. A distinct kind of analysis: funnel and conversion analysis.

A funnel orders stages and measures conversion between them.
Each stage is a filter; drop-off is the complement.
Funnels reveal where a process loses users.
Stage order and definition change the answer — document them.

title: 9  An A/B Test Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that compares two feature variants (for example, a redesigned page or a backend change) with a permutation test and a bootstrap confidence interval for the effect on latency or conversion. A distinct kind of analysis: experimentation and inference.

The null hypothesis is “no real difference”; shuffling labels simulates it.
A p-value is how often shuffles look as extreme as the real data.
The bootstrap puts a confidence interval around an effect size.
Simulated inference replaces closed-form math we may not know.

title: 10  A Forecasting Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that fits simple trend and seasonal models to operational metrics and evaluates them by forecasting the held-out recent past (backtesting). A distinct kind of analysis: forecasting.

A forecast is an extrapolation, and its error grows with the horizon.
Naive and seasonal baselines give a floor to beat.
Backtesting holds out the recent past to judge a model.
Forecast uncertainty matters as much as the point forecast.

title: 11  A Linear Regression Pipeline
text:
Build a least-squares regression pipeline: fit a line to predict a numeric outcome — request latency from load and payload size, or build time from code size — inspect the residuals, and evaluate the fit on held-out data. A distinct kind of analysis: predictive modeling with a continuous outcome.

Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals.
Coefficients have concrete, checkable meanings.
Residuals reveal what the model misses.
A fitted line is a claim, not a fact — evaluate it on unseen data.

title: 12  A Classification Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that predicts a category — will this request fail with a 5xx, or will this build fail? — from its features, and judge it with a confusion matrix and the right metric. A distinct kind of analysis: predictive modeling with a categorical outcome.

Classification predicts a label, not a number.
A confusion matrix shows the kinds of errors a classifier makes.
Accuracy alone misleads when classes are imbalanced.
The right metric depends on the cost of each kind of error.

title: 13  A Similarity Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that finds the records most like a given one — similar error reports, similar services, or similar users — under some distance on chosen features. A distinct kind of analysis: nearest-neighbor and similarity analysis.

“Similar” means close under some distance on chosen features.
Feature choice and scaling decide what similarity means.
Nearest neighbors generalize from “equal” to “nearby”.
Similarity underpins recommendation and record linkage.

title: 14  A Text Analysis Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that tokenizes commit messages or issue titles, counts terms, and scores documents with TF-IDF to find what distinguishes them. A distinct kind of analysis: text mining.

Tokenization and normalization turn free text into countable units.
Term frequency is a start; TF-IDF down-weights common terms.
A document becomes a vector of term weights.
Text pipelines need the same cleaning and validation as numeric ones.

title: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB
text:
Build the same analytical workflow over the event log and users in declarative SQL using DuckDB, and see how a columnar engine differs from dataframe code. A distinct kind of analysis: relational and declarative.

SQL says what you want; the engine decides how to compute it.
SELECT, WHERE, GROUP, and JOIN mirror the dataframe operations already used.
DuckDB’s columnar engine is optimized for analytical queries.
Two mental models — dataframe and relational — solve the same problems.
crumbs: 15  A SQL Pipeline with DuckDB

title: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web
text:
Build an ingestion pipeline that fetches a repository’s issues or commits (or a CI status feed) from a public API with httpx, transforms it, and loads it into DuckDB — handling pagination, rate limits, and caching. A distinct kind of analysis: extract, transform, load.

ETL is ingest → transform → load, and the ingest step is often the web.
httpx fetches; we add pagination, rate limits, and caching around it.
Cache responses so re-runs don’t re-fetch (or re-bill) the source.
A mock server lets us test the pipeline offline.
crumbs: 16  An ETL Pipeline from the Web

title: 17  An Anomaly and Monitoring Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that flags unusual values and detects drift in operational metrics using z-scores and simple control rules. A distinct kind of analysis: monitoring and anomaly detection.

An anomaly is an observation far from what a model expects.
Z-scores and rolling statistics define “expected” and “far”.
Drift means the data’s baseline itself is moving.
Monitoring runs continuously, so it must be cheap and logged.
crumbs: 17  An Anomaly and Monitoring Pipeline

title: 18  A Clustering Pipeline
text:
Build a pipeline that groups records into segments — services by traffic pattern, or users by behavior — with a simple k-means routine and interprets what each cluster means. A distinct kind of analysis: unsupervised segmentation.

Clustering groups records without predefined labels.
k-means alternates assignment and centroid updates until stable.
The algorithm finds structure, not meaning — interpret the clusters.
Validate by asking whether clusters are stable and useful.

title: 19  A Reproducible Pipeline
text:
Build a runner that records each step’s inputs and outputs and re-runs only the steps whose inputs changed, tying provenance and orchestration together. The meta-pipeline that manages the others.

Pipeline steps form a directed graph of dependencies.
A runner re-executes only the steps that are stale.
A recorded pipeline is a reproducible pipeline.
This is how real tools manage analyses end-to-end.

title: Data Analysis Design by Example
text:
Conclusion

Recap the through-line: each lesson built a small version of a real pipeline of a different kind, using mature tools rather than rebuilding them. The habits — verify, document, reproduce — matter more than any single technique, and are what to carry into whatever comes next.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.2 Our Responsibilities
Project maintainers are responsible for clarifying the standards of acceptable behavior and are expected to take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any instances of unacceptable behavior.
Project maintainers have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, or to ban temporarily or permanently any contributor for other behaviors that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.3 Scope
This Code of Conduct applies both within project spaces and in public spaces when an individual is representing the project or its community. Examples of representing a project or community include using an official project email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event. Representation of a project may be further defined and clarified by project maintainers.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.4 Enforcement
Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported by emailing the project team. All complaints will be reviewed and investigated and will result in a response that is deemed necessary and appropriate to the circumstances. The project team is obligated to maintain confidentiality with regard to the reporter of an incident. Further details of specific enforcement policies may be posted separately.
Project maintainers who do not follow or enforce the Code of Conduct in good faith may face temporary or permanent repercussions as determined by other members of the project’s leadership.

title: Appendix B — Code of Conduct
text:
B.5 Attribution
This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant version 1.4.

title: Appendix C — Contributing
text:
C.1 FAQ
Contributions are very welcome; please contact us by email or by filing an issue in our repository. All contributors must abide by our Code of Conduct.

title: Appendix C — Contributing
text:
Do you need help?

Yes—please see the issues in our repository.

What sort of feedback would be useful?

Everything is welcome, from pointing out mistakes to suggestions for better explanations.

Can I add a new section?

Possibly, but please reach out before doing so.

Why is this material free?

Because if we all give a little, we all get a lot.
